titles: Welfare Diplomacy: Benchmarking Language Model Cooperation
keywords: multiagent systems; cooperative AI; AI agents; language models
abstracts: The growing capabilities and increasingly widespread deployment of AI systems necessitate robust benchmarks for measuring their cooperative capabilities. Unfortunately, most multi-agent benchmarks are either zero-sum or purely cooperative, providing limited opportunities for such measurements. We introduce a general-sum variant of the zero-sum board game Diplomacy—called Welfare Diplomacy—in which players must balance investing in military conquest and domestic welfare. We argue that Welfare Diplomacy facilitates both a clearer assessment of and stronger training incentives for cooperative capabilities. Our contributions are: (1) proposing the Welfare Diplomacy rules and implementing them via an open- source Diplomacy engine; (2) constructing baseline agents using zero-shot prompted language models; and (3) conducting experiments where we find that baselines using state-of-the-art models attain high social welfare but are exploitable. Our work aims to promote societal safety by aiding researchers in developing and assessing multi-agent AI systems. Code to evaluate Welfare Diplomacy and reproduce our experiments is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/welfare-diplomacy-72AC.
one_sentence_summary: Our work proposes a general-sum variant of diplomacy to measure the cooperative capabilities of AI agents.
standard_prompt: The authors propose and implement Welfare Diplomacy, a new general-sum variation of the classic two-player strategy game, to measure and incentivize cooperative abilities in artificial intelligence through its application with zero-shot prompting techniques, aiming to improve the evaluation and development of multi-agent AI systems.
cot_prompt: Welfare Diplomacy introduces a new benchmark for cooperative capabilities in multi-agent systems, enabling researchers to assess and improve the social welfare outcomes of AI-powered interactions through an open-source implementation of the game's rules.
dsp_prompt: Welfare Diplomacy introduces a new cooperative benchmark game for AI agents, enabling researchers to measure and improve their ability to balance investment in military conquest and domestic welfare across multiple entities, ultimately promoting safer and more efficient cooperative AI systems.

titles: The Power of Sparsity in Convolutional Neural Networks
keywords: Deep learning; Supervised Learning
abstracts: Deep convolutional networks are well-known for their high computational and memory demands. Given limited resources, how does one design a network that balances its size, training time, and prediction accuracy? A surprisingly effective approach to trade accuracy for size and speed is to simply reduce the number of channels in each convolutional layer by a fixed fraction and retrain the network. In many cases this leads to significantly smaller networks with only minimal changes to accuracy. In this paper, we take a step further by empirically examining a strategy for deactivating connections between filters in convolutional layers in a way that allows us to harvest savings both in run-time and memory for many network architectures. More specifically, we generalize 2D convolution to use a channel-wise sparse connection structure and show that this leads to significantly better results than the baseline approach for large networks including VGG and Inception V3.
one_sentence_summary: Sparse random connections that allow savings to be harvested and that are very effective at compressing CNNs.
standard_prompt: Reducing the number of channels in convolutional layers can lead to smaller, faster, and more accurate deep neural networks, while also saving significant computational resources.
cot_prompt: Reducing the number of channels and selectively activating connections within convolutional layers enables deep neural networks to achieve significant performance improvements while minimizing resource usage.
dsp_prompt: Reducing the number of channels in convolutional layers and using a sparse connection structure achieves significant improvements in computational efficiency and accuracy across various deep neural network architectures.

titles: NEURAL EXECUTION ENGINES
keywords: neural computation; strong generalization; numerical reasoning
abstracts: Turing complete computation and reasoning are often regarded as necessary pre- cursors to general intelligence. There has been a significant body of work studying neural networks that mimic general computation, but these networks fail to generalize to data distributions that are outside of their training set. We study this problem through the lens of fundamental computer science problems: sorting and graph processing. We modify the masking mechanism of a transformer in order to allow them to implement rudimentary functions with strong generalization. We call this model the Neural Execution Engine, and show that it learns, through supervision, to numerically compute the basic subroutines comprising these algorithms with near perfect accuracy. Moreover, it retains this level of accuracy while generalizing to unseen data and long sequences outside of the training distribution.
one_sentence_summary: We propose neural execution engines (NEEs), which leverage a learned mask and supervised execution traces to mimic the functionality of subroutines and demonstrate strong generalization.
standard_prompt: The authors develop the Neural Execution Engine (Nee) by modifying a transformer's masking mechanism to enable it to learn and perform basic numerical computations accurately across various datasets and sequence lengths, demonstrating its ability to generalize effectively beyond its initial training set.
cot_prompt: The authors introduce the Neural Execution Engine, a modified Transformer model capable of learning and implementing numerical computations, demonstrating strong generalization capabilities across various tasks including sorting and graph processing, even when trained only on small datasets.
dsp_prompt: The Neural Execution Engine, inspired by transformer modifications for general-purpose computation, demonstrates superior numerical reasoning capabilities, achieving high accuracy in complex tasks like sorting and graph processing and exhibiting robust generalizability across diverse datasets and sequence lengths.

titles: Soft Token Matching for Interpretable Low-Resource Classification
keywords: low-resource classification; semantic matching; error boosting; text classification; natural language processing
abstracts:
We propose a model to tackle classification tasks in the presence of very little training data. To this aim, we introduce a novel matching mechanism to focus on elements of the input by using vectors that represent semantically meaningful concepts for the task at hand.
By leveraging highlighted portions of the training data, a simple, yet effective, error boosting technique guides the learning process. In practice, it increases the error associated to relevant parts of the input by a given factor. Results on text classification tasks confirm the benefits of the proposed approach in both balanced and unbalanced cases, thus being of practical use when labeling new examples is expensive. In addition, the model is interpretable, as it allows for human inspection of the learned weights.
one_sentence_summary: We propose a model to efficiently tackle low resource classification, which leverages additional information in the input to guide the learning process.
standard_prompt: A novel soft token matching method enhances low-resource classification accuracy through focused vector representations and boosted error correction, making the model interpretable while reducing label acquisition costs.
cot_prompt: A novel soft token matching method enhances low-resource classification through semantic vector representation and error boosting, demonstrating improved performance in both balanced and unbalanced datasets while maintaining interpretability.
dsp_prompt: A novel soft token matching mechanism enhances low-resource text classification through semantic vector representation and error boosting, achieving interpretability while improving performance in various scenarios.

titles: Ferret: Refer and Ground Anything Anywhere at Any Granularity
keywords: Ferret; Multimodal Large Language Model; Referring; Grounding
abstracts: We introduce Ferret, a new Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) capable of understanding spatial referring of any shape or granularity within an image and accurately grounding open-vocabulary descriptions. To unify referring and grounding in the LLM paradigm, Ferret employs a novel and powerful hybrid region representation that integrates discrete coordinates and continuous features jointly to represent a region in the image. To extract the continuous features of versatile regions,  we propose a spatial-aware visual sampler, adept at handling varying sparsity across different shapes. Consequently, Ferret can accept diverse region inputs, such as points, bounding boxes, and free-form shapes. To bolster the desired capability of Ferret, we curate GRIT, a comprehensive refer-and-ground instruction tuning dataset including 1.1M samples that contain rich hierarchical spatial knowledge, with an additional 130K hard negative data to promote model robustness. The resulting model not only achieves superior performance in classical referring and grounding tasks, but also greatly outperforms existing MLLMs in region-based and localization-demanded multimodal chatting. Our evaluations also reveal a significantly improved capability of describing image details and a remarkable alleviation in object hallucination.
one_sentence_summary: Ferret, a new Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) capable of understanding spatial referring of any shape or granularity within an image and accurately grounding open-vocabulary descriptions.
standard_prompt: Ferret, a novel multimodal language model, unifies referring and grounding capabilities through a hybrid region representation and spatial-aware visual sampling, achieving superior performance in both classical referring and grounding tasks while demonstrating enhanced detail description and reduced object hallucination compared to existing models.
cot_prompt: Ferret, a multimodal large language model, unifies spatial referencing and grounding capabilities through a novel hybrid region representation and spatial-aware visual sampling technique, demonstrating superior performance in various tasks compared to existing models.
dsp_prompt: Ferret, a novel Multimodal Large Language Model, excels in understanding spatial referencing and accurately grounding open-vocabulary descriptions through its innovative hybrid region representation and spatial-aware visual sampling techniques, achieving superior performance over existing models in both classic referring and grounding tasks while demonstrating enhanced detail description capabilities and reduced object hallucination issues.

titles: Contrastive Quant: Quantization Makes Stronger Contrastive Learning
keywords: Contrastive learning; quantization
abstracts: Contrastive learning, which learns visual representations by enforcing feature consistency under different augmented views, has emerged as one of the most effective unsupervised learning methods. In this work, we explore contrastive learning from a new perspective, inspired by the recent works showing that properly designed weight perturbations or quantization help the models learn a smoother loss landscape. Interestingly, we find that quantization, when properly engineered, can enhance the effectiveness of contrastive learning. To this end, we propose a novel contrastive learning framework, dubbed Contrastive Quant, to encourage the feature consistency under both (1) differently augmented inputs via various data transformations and (2) differently augmented weights/activations via various quantization levels, where the feature consistency under injected noises via quantization can be viewed as augmentations on both model weights and intermediate activations as a complement to the input augmentations. Extensive experiments, built on top of two state-of-the-art contrastive learning methods SimCLR and BYOL, show that Contrastive Quant consistently improves the learned visual representation, especially with limited labeled data under semi-supervised scenarios. For example, our Contrastive Quant achieves a 8.69% and 10.27% higher accuracy on ResNet-18 and ResNet-34, respectively, on ImageNet when fine-tuning with 10% labeled data. We believe this work has opened up a new perspective for future contrastive learning innovations. All codes will be released upon acceptance.
one_sentence_summary: We propose the Contrastive Quant framework to further encourage the feature consistency under differently augmented weights/activations via various quantization levels on top of existing contrastive learning methods.
standard_prompt: Contrastive Quant, leveraging proper weight quantization, enhances the effectiveness of contrastive learning through diverse data augmentation strategies, leading to improved visual representation quality across various tasks and settings.
cot_prompt: Contrastive Quant, leveraging quantization techniques, enhances the robustness and efficiency of contrastive learning, particularly improving image classification accuracy through semi-supervised training on limited labeled data.
dsp_prompt: Contrastive Quant's innovative approach leveraging proper weight perturbations and quantization significantly enhances the effectiveness of contrastive learning, improving feature consistency across different inputs and activations, leading to enhanced performance in supervised learning tasks, particularly benefiting semi-supervised scenarios.

titles: Revealing the Structure of Deep Neural Networks via Convex Duality
keywords: Convex optimization; non-convex optimization; deep learning; convex duality; regularization; ReLU activation; linear networks
abstracts: We study regularized deep neural networks (DNNs) and introduce a convex analytic framework to characterize the structure of the hidden layers. We show that a set of optimal hidden layer weights for a norm regularized DNN training problem can be explicitly found as the extreme points of a convex set. For the special case of deep linear networks with $K$ outputs, we prove that each optimal weight matrix is rank-$K$ and aligns with the previous layers via duality. More importantly, we apply the same characterization to deep ReLU networks with whitened data and prove the same weight alignment holds. As a corollary, we prove that norm regularized deep ReLU networks yield spline interpolation for one-dimensional datasets which was previously known only for two-layer networks. Furthermore, we provide closed-form solutions for the optimal layer weights when data is rank-one or whitened. We then verify our theory via numerical experiments.
one_sentence_summary: We study norm regularized deep neural networks and develop a framework based on convex duality such that a set of optimal solutions to the training problem can be explicitly and analytically characterized.
standard_prompt: We develop a convex dual approach to analyze the structure of deep neural networks, showing how optimal weights align across layers in various types of networks, including ReLU networks, and demonstrate applications through theoretical results and numerical examples.
cot_prompt: We develop a convex analytic framework to reveal the structure of hidden layers in deep neural networks through optimal weight matrices, showing their alignment across layers and proving connections to spline interpolation for one-dimensional datasets.
dsp_prompt: We develop a convex analytic framework to characterize the structure of deep neural network weights through optimal hidden layer weights for norm regularized training problems, proving their alignment with previous layers via duality and providing closed-form solutions for specific cases.

titles: Conditional Generative Models are Sufficient to Sample from Any Causal Effect Estimand
keywords: Causality; Causal inference; Structural causal models; Causal graphs; Causal effect; Generative models; Diffusion models
abstracts: The ability to apply causal reasoning from observational data has made causal inference algorithms widely adopted in machine learning applications. While there exist sound and complete algorithms to compute causal effects, these algorithms require explicit access to conditional likelihoods over the observational distribution. In the high dimensional regime, conditional likelihoods are difficult to estimate. To alleviate this issue, researchers have approached the causal effect estimation problem by simulating causal relations with neural models. However, none of these existing approaches can be applied to generic scenarios such as causal graphs having latent confounders and obtaining conditional interventional samples.  In this paper, we show that any identifiable causal effect given an arbitrary causal graph containing latent confounders can be computed through push-forward computations using trained conditional generative models. Based on this observation, we devise a diffusion-based approach to sample from any such interventional or conditional interventional distribution. To showcase our algorithm's performance, we conduct experiments on a semi-synthetic Colored MNIST dataset having both the intervention ($X$) and the target variable ($Y$) as images and present interventional image samples from $P(Y|do(X))$. We also perform a case study on a real-world COVIDx chest X-ray image dataset to demonstrate our algorithm's utility.
one_sentence_summary: We propose a diffusion-based approach to sample from any identifiable interventional or conditional interventional distribution given an arbitrary causal graph containing latent confounders.
standard_prompt: Conditional Generative Models enable computation of any identifiable causal effect from arbitrary graphical causal models with latent confounders, overcoming limitations in estimating conditional likelihoods for high-dimensional datasets.
cot_prompt: Conditional Generative Models enable sampling from any causal effect estimand by leveraging trained models to simulate causal relationships, overcoming limitations in estimating conditional likelihoods for high-dimensional data.
dsp_prompt: Conditional generative models enable the computation of causal effects in complex, latent-confounded causal graphs by leveraging trained models for push-forward operations, facilitating sampling from desired distributions like conditional interventions.

titles: Token Turing Machines
keywords: memory; Neural Turing Machine; robot learning; sequence
abstracts: We propose Token Turing Machines (TTM), a sequential, autoregressive Transformer model with memory for real-world sequential decision making. Our model is inspired by the seminal Neural Turing Machine, and has an external memory consisting of a set of tokens which summarise the previous history. This memory is efficiently addressed, read and written using a Transformer as the processing unit/controller at each step. The model's memory module ensures that a new observation will only be processed with the contents of the memory (and not the entire history), meaning that it can efficiently process long sequences with a bounded computational cost at each step. We show that TTM outperforms other alternatives, such as other Transformer models designed for long sequences and recurrent neural networks, on two real-world sequential decision making tasks: online temporal activity localization from videos and vision-based robot action policy learning.
one_sentence_summary: Token Turing Machines (TTM) is a sequential, autoregressive transformer model with memory for real-world sequential decision making, modernizing Neural Turing Machines.
standard_prompt: Token Turing Machines (TTMs) integrate memory through token summaries to address historical data more efficiently, achieving superior performance in long-sequence decision-making tasks like video analysis and robotic action learning compared to traditional Transformers.
cot_prompt: Token Turing Machines (TTM) combines elements of Transformers and Neural Turing Machines, utilizing a memory system composed of tokens to efficiently process long sequences in real-world sequential decision-making tasks like video analysis and robotic action learning, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional models.
dsp_prompt: The proposed Token Turing Machine (TTM) combines elements of the Neural Turing Machine with a transformer architecture, utilizing a memory system composed of tokens to efficiently handle long sequences in real-world sequential decision-making tasks like video analysis and robot action policy learning.

titles: Self-Architectural Knowledge Distillation for Spiking Neural Networks
keywords: Spiking Neural Networks; Knowledge Distillation; Neural Architecture Search
abstracts: Brain-inspired spiking neural networks (SNNs) have drawn wide attention recently since they are biologically plausible and neuromorphic hardware-friendly. To obtain low-latency (i.e., a small number of timesteps) SNNs, the surrogate gradients (SG) method has been widely applied. However, SNNs trained by the SG method still have a huge performance gap from artificial neural networks (ANNs). In this paper, we find that the knowledge distillation paradigm can effectively alleviate the performance gap by transferring the knowledge from ANNs (teacher) to SNNs (student), but it remains a problem to find the architecture of teacher-student pairs. We introduce neural architecture search (NAS) and find that the performance is insensitive to the architectures of SNNs. Hence, we choose the same architecture for ANN-teacher and SNN-student since it is easy to implement and the student can initiate the weight from the teacher. We thus propose a Self-Architectural Knowledge Distillation framework (SAKD), which matches the knowledge (i.e., the features and logits) of ANNs to that of SNNs with the same architecture. Although adopting a teacher model in training, SNNs trained via our SAKD still keep ultra-low latency (T=4) compared with other methods and achieve state-of-the-art performance on a variety of datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and DVS-CIFAR10), and we demonstrate that this simple training strategy can provide a new training paradigm of SNNs.
one_sentence_summary: We propose a Self-Architectural Knowledge Distillation framework (SAKD), which matches the knowledge (i.e., the features and logits) of ANNs to that of SNNs with the same architecture.
standard_prompt: The authors propose Self-Architectural Knowledge Distillation (SAKD), a novel approach that leverages neural architecture search to transfer knowledge between artificial neural networks (teachers) and spike-based neural networks (students) using a shared architecture, achieving ultra-low latency while maintaining competitive performance across various benchmark datasets.
cot_prompt: A novel Self-Architectural Knowledge Distillation (SAKD) framework combines the knowledge transfer from artificial neural networks (ANNs) to spiking neural networks (SNNs) using NAS, achieving ultra-low latency (T=4) while maintaining competitive performance across various datasets.
dsp_prompt: The Self-Architectural Knowledge Distillation framework leverages neural architecture search and knowledge transfer between artificial neural networks and spiking neural networks, achieving ultra-low latency while maintaining high accuracy across various datasets through a simple training strategy.

titles: Beyond Scale: the Diversity Coefficient as a Data Quality Metric Demonstrates LLMs are Pre-trained on Formally Diverse Data
keywords: machine learning; large language models; metrics; data diversity; data; data quality
abstracts: Current trends to pre-train capable Large Language Models (LLMs) mostly focus on scaling of model and dataset size. However, the of pre-training data is an important factor for training powerful LLMs, yet it is a nebulous concept that has not been fully characterized. Therefore, we use the recently proposed Task2Vec diversity coefficient to understand formal aspects of data \textit{quality} that go beyond scale alone. Specifically, we measure the diversity coefficient of publicly available pre-training datasets to demonstrate that their formal diversity is high when compared to theoretical lower and upper bounds. In addition, to build confidence in the diversity coefficient, we conduct interpretability experiments and find that the coefficient aligns with intuitive properties of diversity, e.g., it increases as the number of latent concepts increases. We conclude the diversity coefficient is reliable and conjecture it can be used to build useful diverse datasets for LLMs.
one_sentence_summary: We rigorously test a formal quantitive metric for data diversity for LLMs and conjecture it helps downstream performance
standard_prompt: The Task2Vec diversity coefficient effectively measures the quality of pre-training data for large language models, demonstrating significant formal diversity across various datasets, thereby supporting its potential use in creating more varied and informative training sets for AI applications.
cot_prompt: The Task2Vec diversity coefficient demonstrates high formal data quality in pre-training datasets for large language models, showing increased diversity with more latent concepts.
dsp_prompt: The Task2Vec diversity coefficient reveals high formal data diversity among pre-training datasets for large language models, supporting its reliability for building more varied and effective training sets.

titles: Provably convergent quasistatic dynamics for mean-field two-player zero-sum games
keywords: quasistatic; minimax optimization; mixed Nash equilibrium; mean-field formulation
abstracts: In this paper, we study the problem of finding mixed Nash equilibrium for mean-field two-player zero-sum games. Solving this problem requires optimizing over two probability distributions. We consider a quasistatic Wasserstein gradient flow dynamics in which one probability distribution follows the Wasserstein gradient flow, while the other one is always at the equilibrium. Theoretical analysis are conducted on this dynamics, showing its convergence to the mixed Nash equilibrium under mild conditions. Inspired by the continuous dynamics of probability distributions, we derive a quasistatic Langevin gradient descent method with inner-outer iterations, and test the method on different problems, including training mixture of GANs.
one_sentence_summary: We propose a quasistatic Wasserstein flow for finding mixed Nash equilibriums, and prove its convergence.
standard_prompt: A novel quasistatic dynamics approach, based on Wasserstein gradient flows, is developed to converge to mixed Nash equilibria for mean-field two-player zero-sum games through theoretical analysis and practical application, specifically designed for training mixtures of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).
cot_prompt: In this paper, researchers develop a quasistatic dynamical system for solving mean-field two-player zero-sum games, demonstrating its convergence to the mixed Nash equilibrium through theoretical analysis and practical application to training mixtures of Generative Adversarial Networks.
dsp_prompt: In this work, we investigate mean-field two-player zero-sum games using a quasistatic Wasserstein gradient flow dynamics, proving its convergence to the mixed Nash equilibrium through theoretical analysis and practical application in minimizing the difference between two probability distributions.

titles: Trustless Audits without Revealing Data or Models
keywords: trustless audit; zero-knowledge proof
abstracts:
There is an increasing conflict between business incentives to hide models and data as trade secrets, and the societal need for algorithmic transparency. For example, a rightsholder who currently wishes to know whether their copyrighted works have been used during training must convince the model provider to allow a third party to audit the model and data. Finding a mutually agreeable third party is difficult, and the associated costs often make this approach impractical.

In this work, we show that it is possible to simultaneously allow model providers to keep their models and data secret while allowing other parties to trustlessly audit properties of the model and data. We do this by designing a protocol called ZkAudit in which model providers publish cryptographic commitments of datasets and model weights, alongside a zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) certifying that published commitments are derived from training the model. Model providers can then respond to audit requests by privately computing any function F of the dataset (or model) and releasing the output of F alongside another ZKP certifying the correct execution of F. To enable ZkAudit, we develop new methods of computing ZKPs for SGD on modern neural nets for recommender systems and image classification models capable of high accuracies on ImageNet. Empirically, we show it is possible to provide trustless audits of DNNs, including copyright, censorship, and counterfactual audits with little to no loss in accuracy.
one_sentence_summary: We enable trustless audits of recommender systems and high-accuracy image models for the first time
standard_prompt: A novel protocol, ZkAudit, enables model providers to maintain confidentiality while allowing trusted auditors to verify DNN properties such as copyright, censorship, and counterfactual scenarios using secure multi-party computation techniques, demonstrating its effectiveness through practical applications in various domains.
cot_prompt: Our work introduces ZkAudit, a novel protocol that allows model providers to maintain privacy while enabling trusted audits through zk-SNARKs, facilitating tasks like copyright and censorship verification with minimal performance degradation.
dsp_prompt: A novel protocol named ZkAudit enables model providers to maintain confidentiality while allowing trusted third parties to verify DNN properties like copyright violations, censorship, and counterfactuals through secure multiparty computation and zero-knowledge proofs, achieving privacy-preserving audits at near-original performance levels.

titles: ONLINE RESTLESS BANDITS WITH UNOBSERVED STATES
keywords: Thompson Sampling; Explore-Then-Commit; online restless bandit
abstracts: We study the online restless bandit problem, where each arm evolves according to a Markov chain independently, and the reward of pulling an arm depends on both the current state of the corresponding Markov chain and the action. The agent (decision maker) does not know the transition kernels and reward functions, and cannot observe the states of arms all the time.  The goal is to sequentially choose which arms to pull so as to maximize the expected cumulative rewards collected.  In this paper, we propose TSEETC, a learning algorithm based on Thompson Sampling with Episodic Explore-Then-Commit. The algorithm proceeds in episodes of increasing length and each episode is divided into exploration and exploitation phases. In the exploration phase in each episode, action-reward samples are collected in a round-robin way and then used to update the posterior as a mixture of Dirichlet distributions.  At the beginning of the exploitation phase, TSEETC generates a sample from the posterior distribution as true parameters. It then follows the optimal policy for the sampled model for the rest of the episode. We establish the Bayesian regret bound $\tilde {\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ for TSEETC, where $T$ is the time horizon. This is the first bound that is close to the lower bound of restless bandits, especially in an unobserved state setting. We show through simulations that TSEETC outperforms existing algorithms in regret.
one_sentence_summary: We propose TSEETC to slove the restless bandits with unknown transition kernels,unknown reward functions and unobserved states.
standard_prompt: In the online restless bandit problem, TSEETC, a Thompson Sampling-based approach combining exploration and exploitation over episodes, achieves near-optimal performance with a Bayesian regret bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$, demonstrating superior performance over existing methods particularly in the unobserved state scenario.
cot_prompt: We propose TSEETC, a Thompson Sampling-based algorithm for the online restless bandit problem with unknown states, achieving near-optimal regret bounds and superior performance over existing methods in simulations.
dsp_prompt: In the online restless bandit problem with unobserved states, TSEETC, a Thompson Sampling-based algorithm, achieves near-optimal performance by adaptively exploring different models during its episodes, demonstrating superior regret over existing methods.

titles: FACE SUPER-RESOLUTION GUIDED BY 3D FACIAL PRIORS
keywords: Super-resolution; 3D Facial priors; Spatial Attention Mechanism
abstracts: State-of-the-art face super-resolution methods employ deep convolutional neural networks to learn a mapping between low- and high-resolution facial patterns by exploring local appearance knowledge. However, most of these methods do not well exploit facial structures and identity information, and struggle to deal with facial images that exhibit large pose variation and misalignment. In this paper, we propose a novel face super-resolution method that explicitly incorporates 3D facial priors which grasp the sharp facial structures. Firstly, the 3D face rendering branch is set up to obtain 3D priors of salient facial structures and identity knowledge. Secondly, the Spatial Attention Mechanism is used to better exploit this hierarchical information (i.e. intensity similarity, 3D facial structure, identity content) for the super-resolution problem. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves superior face super-resolution results and outperforms the state-of-the-art.
one_sentence_summary: We propose a novel face super resolution method that explicitly incorporates 3D facial priors which grasp the sharp facial structures.
standard_prompt: A new face super-resolution method using 3D facial priors and spatial attention demonstrates superior performance over current state-of-the-art techniques by effectively integrating local appearance and structural information.
cot_prompt: The proposed method integrates 3D facial priors to enhance the spatial attention mechanism in face super-resolution, achieving superior performance over existing techniques.
dsp_prompt: The proposed method leverages 3D facial priors and a spatial attention mechanism to enhance super-resolution performance, particularly for capturing sharp facial features and handling diverse poses effectively.

titles: Harnessing the Power of Large Language Models for Natural Language to First-Order Logic Translation
keywords: Large Language Models; Natrual Language to First-Order Logic Translation
abstracts:
Translating natural language sentences to first-order logic (NL-FOL translation) remains a critical task in many logic-based NLP systems, as it enables ML models to reason logically over text.
However, existing translation methods still struggle to scale to real-world tasks due to the lack of a large and high-quality dataset and a model family with high precision and coverage.

In this work, we approach this longstanding challenge by harnessing the power of pre-trained large language models (LLMs).
To do so, we present MALLS (large language **M**odel gener**A**ted N**L**-FO**L** pair**S**), a dataset of 28K diverse and verified sentence-level NL-FOL pairs collected from GPT-4.
We create MALLS by implementing an adaptive pipeline that prompts GPT-4 for pairs with rich and diverse contexts. 
To ensure the validity of FOL rules and their alignment with the NL sentences, we utilized a combined strategy of FOL rule parsing, human annotation, and automatic filtering.

We also present LogicLLaMA, an LLaMA2-7B/13B model family fine-tuned on MALLS for NL-FOL translation. 
LogicLLaMA is capable of directly translating natural language into FOL rules, which outperforms GPT-3.5. 
LogicLLaMA is also equipped to correct FOL rules predicted by GPT-3.5, and can achieve similar performance as GPT-4 with a fraction of the cost.
This correction ability was achieved by a novel reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) framework, which initially trains on synthetically perturbed NL-FOL pairs to encourage chain-of-thought reasoning and then fine-tunes with RLHF on GPT-3.5 outputs using a FOL verifier as the reward model. 
Codes and data are available [here](https://www.dropbox.com/sh/t0f69776773e9er/AABKaWuvepUvhSp-0u2w-b2Pa?dl=0).
one_sentence_summary: We collect and verfiy a large NL-FOL pair dataset from GPT4; we finetune LLaMA-7B/13B models on this dataset which yields GPT-4 level performance
standard_prompt: Large language models like GPT-4 were used to generate millions of NL-FOL pairs through an adaptive pipeline, leading to the creation of MALLS. The resulting dataset enabled the development of LogicLLaMA, an LLaMA2-7B/13B model family fine-tuned specifically for NL-FOL translation, demonstrating improved accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional approaches.
cot_prompt: Large language models like GPT-4 are leveraged to generate a large dataset of NL-FOL pairs through an adaptive pipeline that incorporates FOL rule parsing, human annotation, and automated filtering. LogicLLaMA, a fine-tuned version of LLaMA2, translates NL sentences to FOL rules, achieving superior accuracy compared to GPT-3.5 while correcting predictions made by GPT-3.5 using a reinforcement learning method. The research contributes to the field of natural language processing by enhancing logical reasoning capabilities through the integration of machine learning techniques and human feedback.
dsp_prompt: Large Language Models like GPT-4 were used to collect 28K NL-FOL pairs through an adaptive pipeline, leading to the creation of MALLS and the development of LogicLLaMA, an improved version of LLaMA2-7B/13B trained specifically for NL-FOL translation, showcasing its potential in correcting predictions made by GPT-3.

titles: Approximation capability of neural networks on sets of probability measures and tree-structured data
keywords: multi-instance learning; hierarchical models; universal approximation theorem
abstracts:
This paper extends the proof of density of neural networks in the space of continuous (or even measurable) functions on Euclidean spaces to functions on compact sets of probability measures.
By doing so the work parallels a more then a decade old results on mean-map embedding of probability measures in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces.  
The work has wide practical consequences for multi-instance learning, where it theoretically justifies some recently proposed constructions.
The result is then extended to Cartesian products, yielding universal approximation theorem for tree-structured domains, which naturally occur in data-exchange formats like JSON, XML, YAML, AVRO, and ProtoBuffer. This has important practical implications, as it enables to automatically create an architecture of neural networks for processing structured data (AutoML paradigms), as demonstrated by an accompanied library for JSON format.
one_sentence_summary: This paper extends the proof of density of neural networks in the space of continuous (or even measurable) functions on Euclidean spaces to functions on compact sets of probability measures.
standard_prompt: This paper generalizes neural network approximation capabilities to compact sets of probability measures and tree-structured data, extending previous results and enabling automatic architecture creation for structured data exchange formats.
