cot_prompt: In this study, researchers develop a GAM-based model using what-if scenarios to predict expert goals in batch IRL for healthcare, demonstrating superior performance over traditional methods like linear regression and providing clinically aligned explanations.
dsp_prompt: Explainable, interpretable, and accurate GAM-based what-if future outcome reasoning enhances inverse reinforcement learning for recovering expert goals in healthcare, demonstrating consistency with clinical guidelines and overcoming limitations of traditional metrics like matched action accuracy.

titles: Improving Graph Neural Network Expressivity via Subgraph Isomorphism Counting
keywords: graph neural networks; graph representation learning; network analysis; network motifs; subgraph isomoprhism
abstracts: While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable results in a variety of applications, recent studies exposed important shortcomings in their ability to capture the structure of the underlying graph. It has been shown that the expressive power of standard GNNs is bounded by the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) graph isomorphism test, from which they inherit proven limitations such as the inability to detect and count graph substructures. On the other hand, there is significant empirical evidence, e.g. in network science and bioinformatics, that substructures are often informative for downstream tasks, suggesting that it is desirable to design GNNs capable of leveraging this important source of information. To this end, we propose a novel topologically-aware message passing scheme based on substructure encoding. We show that our architecture allows incorporating domain-specific inductive biases and that it is strictly more expressive than the WL test. Importantly, in contrast to recent works on the expressivity of GNNs, we do not attempt to adhere to the WL hierarchy; this allows us to retain multiple attractive properties of standard GNNs such as locality and linear network complexity, while being able to disambiguate even hard instances of graph isomorphism. We extensively evaluate our method on graph classification and regression tasks and show state-of-the-art results on multiple datasets including molecular graphs and social networks.
one_sentence_summary: We show that enhancing message passing neural networks with subgraph encodings improves their expressive power and allows incorporating domain specific prior knowledge
standard_prompt: Our novel topologically-aware message-passing scheme surpasses the Weisfeiler-Lehman hierarchy's expressivity bounds, enabling efficient detection and counting of subgraphs in Graph Neural Networks, achieving superior performance across various graph classification and regression tasks.
cot_prompt: Our novel GNN architecture surpasses the Weisfeiler-Lehman isomorphism test's expressivity bounds through substructure encoding, achieving superior performance on graph classification and regression tasks, including challenging cases of graph isomorphism.
dsp_prompt: Our proposed topologically-aware GNN architecture, inspired by substructure encoding, surpasses the Weisfeiler-Lehman hierarchy's expressivity, enabling precise graph isomorphism disambiguation and superior performance in graph classification and regression tasks through domain-specific inductive biases.

titles: Statestream: A toolbox to explore layerwise-parallel deep neural networks
keywords: model-parallel; parallelization; software platform
abstracts: Building deep neural networks to control autonomous agents which have to interact in real-time with the physical world, such as robots or automotive vehicles, requires a seamless integration of time into a network’s architecture. The central question of this work is, how the temporal nature of reality should be reflected in the execution of a deep neural network and its components. Most artificial deep neural networks are partitioned into a directed graph of connected modules or layers and the layers themselves consist of elemental building blocks, such as single units. For most deep neural networks, all units of a layer are processed synchronously and in parallel, but layers themselves are processed in a sequential manner. In contrast, all elements of a biological neural network are processed in parallel. In this paper, we define a class of networks between these two extreme cases. These networks are executed in a streaming or synchronous layerwise-parallel manner, unlocking the layers of such networks for parallel processing. Compared to the standard layerwise-sequential deep networks, these new layerwise-parallel networks show a fundamentally different temporal behavior and flow of information, especially for networks with skip or recurrent connections. We argue that layerwise-parallel deep networks are better suited for future challenges of deep neural network design, such as large functional modularized and/or recurrent architectures as well as networks allocating different network capacities dependent on current stimulus and/or task complexity. We layout basic properties and discuss major challenges for layerwise-parallel networks. Additionally, we provide a toolbox to design, train, evaluate, and online-interact with layerwise-parallel networks.
one_sentence_summary: We define a concept of layerwise model-parallel deep neural networks, for which layers operate in parallel, and provide a toolbox to design, train, evaluate, and on-line interact with these networks.
standard_prompt: The study introduces Layerwise-Parallel Deep Neural Networks (LPDNNs), a novel architecture that processes layers sequentially within each individual unit but simultaneously across layers, offering a balance between computational efficiency and parallelism over traditional deep neural networks.
cot_prompt: The study introduces LayerStream, a novel type of deep neural network that processes layers in a layered, synchronized fashion, enabling parallel computation and offering advantages over traditional sequential architectures by mimicking biological neural network principles.
dsp_prompt: This research introduces LayerStream (Layerwise Stream), a novel architecture for deep neural networks that processes individual layers in parallel within a streaming framework, offering advantages over traditional sequential models through improved scalability and adaptability in complex tasks.

titles: Online Hyperparameter Meta-Learning with Hypergradient Distillation
keywords: Hyperparameter Optimization; Meta-learning
abstracts: Many gradient-based meta-learning methods assume a set of parameters that do not participate in inner-optimization, which can be considered as hyperparameters. Although such hyperparameters can be optimized using the existing gradient-based hyperparameter optimization (HO) methods, they suffer from the following issues. Unrolled differentiation methods do not scale well to high-dimensional hyperparameters or horizon length, Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) based methods are restrictive for online optimization, and short horizon approximations suffer from short horizon bias. In this work, we propose a novel HO method that can overcome these limitations, by approximating the second-order term with knowledge distillation. Specifically, we parameterize a single Jacobian-vector product (JVP) for each HO step and minimize the distance from the true second-order term. Our method allows online optimization and also is scalable to the hyperparameter dimension and the horizon length. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three different meta-learning methods and two benchmark datasets.
one_sentence_summary: We propose a gradient-based hyperparameter optimization method based on the idea of knowledge distillation, which is fully online and applicable to high-dimensional hyperparameters.
standard_prompt: Our proposed HO method optimizes hyperparameters through knowledge distillation, enabling online optimization and scalability across high-dimensional and long-horizon scenarios.
cot_prompt: Our proposed HO method, parameterized by JVPs, enables online optimization and scalability while minimizing the distance to the true second-order term through knowledge distillation, overcoming limitations in unrolled differentiation and IFT-based approaches.
dsp_prompt: Our proposed HO method, utilizing knowledge distillation to approximate the second-order term, addresses scalability challenges in online hyperparameter optimization, enabling efficient and effective hyperparameter tuning across diverse meta-learning scenarios.

titles: DeFINE: Deep Factorized Input Token Embeddings for Neural Sequence Modeling
keywords: sequence modeling; input representations; language modeling; word embedding
abstracts: For sequence models with large vocabularies, a majority of network parameters lie in the input and output layers. In this work, we describe a new method, DeFINE, for learning deep token representations efficiently. Our architecture uses a hierarchical structure with novel skip-connections which allows for the use of low dimensional input and output layers, reducing total parameters and training time while delivering similar or better performance versus existing methods. DeFINE can be incorporated easily in new or existing sequence models. Compared to state-of-the-art methods including adaptive input representations, this technique results in a 6% to 20% drop in perplexity. On WikiText-103, DeFINE reduces the total parameters of Transformer-XL by half with minimal impact on performance. On the Penn Treebank, DeFINE improves AWD-LSTM by 4 points with a 17% reduction in parameters, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods with fewer parameters. For machine translation, DeFINE improves the efficiency of the Transformer model by about 1.4 times while delivering similar performance.
one_sentence_summary: DeFINE uses a deep, hierarchical, sparse network with new skip connections to learn better word embeddings efficiently.
standard_prompt: DeFINE, an efficient method using a hierarchical structure with novel skip-connections, significantly reduces parameter counts and improves performance in neural sequence modeling tasks such as language translation and natural language processing, achieving up to 20% improvement over state-of-the-art techniques.
cot_prompt: DeFINE, a novel architecture for neural sequence modeling, achieves significant parameter savings through efficient representation learning and reduced dimensions, demonstrating improvements over state-of-the-art methods across various tasks including language processing and machine translation.
dsp_prompt: DeFINE, a novel deep factorized input token embedding approach, leverages a hierarchical structure and skip-connections to efficiently learn compact representations for large vocabulary sequence models, significantly reducing parameter counts and improving performance across various tasks including language modeling, text classification, and machine translation.

titles: Revisiting Global Pooling through the Lens of Optimal Transport
keywords: Global pooling; regularized optimal transport; Bregman ADMM; multi-instance learning; graph embedding
abstracts: Global pooling is one of the most significant operations in many machine learning models and tasks, whose implementation, however, is often empirical in practice. In this study, we develop a novel and solid global pooling framework through the lens of optimal transport. We demonstrate that most existing global pooling methods are equivalent to solving some specializations of an unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) problem. Making the parameters of the UOT problem learnable, we unify various global pooling methods in the same framework, and accordingly, propose a generalized global pooling layer called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) for neural networks. Besides implementing the UOTP layer based on the classic Sinkhorn-scaling algorithm, we design new model architectures based on the Bregman ADMM algorithm, which has comparable complexity but better numerical stability. We test our UOTP layers in several application scenarios, including multi-instance learning, graph classification, and image classification. In these applications, our UOTP layers can either imitate conventional global pooling layers or learn new pooling mechanisms to perform better.
one_sentence_summary: We develop a novel and solid global pooling framework through the lens of optimal transport, which covers many existing pooling methods and performs well on various learning problems.
standard_prompt: The authors develop the UOT-Pooling (UOTP) layer, unified by the unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) problem, demonstrating its equivalence to existing global pooling methods and proposing new model architectures with improved numerical stability over traditional approaches.
cot_prompt: Our study proposes a unified framework, the UOT-Pooling (UOTP), based on optimal transport theory, which simplifies and generalizes multiple global pooling techniques by making their parameters learnable, leading to improved performance across diverse applications like multi-instance learning, graph classification, and image classification.
dsp_prompt: Our study introduces the Unified Optimal Transport Pooling (UOTP) layer, unified by learning parameters of the Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) problem, demonstrating its equivalence to multiple global pooling techniques while achieving better performance in applications like multi-instance learning, graph classification, and image classification.

titles: Efficient and Scalable Graph Generation through Iterative Local Expansion
keywords: Graph Generation; Denoising Diffusion; Spectral Graph Theory
abstracts:
In the realm of generative models for graphs, extensive research has been conducted. However, most existing methods struggle with large graphs due to the complexity of representing the entire joint distribution across all node pairs and capturing both global and local graph structures simultaneously.
To overcome these issues, we introduce a method that generates a graph by progressively expanding a single node to a target graph. In each step, nodes and edges are added in a localized manner through denoising diffusion, building first the global structure, and then refining the local details. The local generation avoids modeling the entire joint distribution over all node pairs, achieving substantial computational savings with subquadratic runtime relative to node count while maintaining high expressivity through multiscale generation.
Our experiments show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on well-established benchmark datasets while successfully scaling to graphs with at least 5000 nodes. Our method is also the first to successfully extrapolate to graphs outside of the training distribution, showcasing a much better generalization capability over existing methods.
one_sentence_summary: We introduce a novel method to build a graph by progressively expanding a single node to a target graph, adding nodes and edges in a localized manner through denoising diffusion, building first the global structure and then refining.
standard_prompt: We present a novel iterative local expansion approach for generating efficient and scalable graphs, significantly reducing computation time and improving performance compared to existing methods.
cot_prompt: We present an iterative local expansion algorithm for generating efficient and scalable graphs, demonstrating superior performance on large-scale datasets compared to existing methods.
dsp_prompt: We present a novel iterative local expansion approach to efficiently generate large-scale graphs using denoising diffusion, significantly reducing computational cost and enhancing scalability compared to existing methods.

titles: FairGrad: Fairness Aware Gradient Descent
keywords: Group Fairness; Optimization
abstracts: We address the problem of group fairness in classification, where the objective is to learn models that do not unjustly discriminate against subgroups of the population. Most existing approaches are limited to simple binary tasks or involve difficult to implement training mechanisms. This reduces their practical applicability. In this paper, we propose FairGrad, a method to enforce fairness based on a reweighting scheme that iteratively learns group specific weights based on whether they are advantaged or not. FairGrad is easy to implement and can accommodate various standard fairness definitions. Furthermore, we show that it is competitive with standard baselines over various datasets including ones used in natural language processing and computer vision.
one_sentence_summary: A method to enforce fairness based on a reweighting scheme that iteratively learns group specific weights based on whether they are advantaged or not.
standard_prompt: FairGrad is a gradient descent-based approach that reweights gradients during learning to ensure fair treatment across different groups, offering ease of implementation and versatility for various fairness criteria.
cot_prompt: FairGrad introduces a reweighting scheme for gradient descent to enforce fairness in classification, enabling practical application through ease-of-implementation and flexibility in accommodating different fairness definitions across various domains, showing competitive performance compared to traditional methods.
dsp_prompt: FairGrad, a gradient descent-based approach, reweights data for fair classification by optimizing group-specific weights while maintaining competitiveness with traditional fairness methods across diverse applications.

titles: Building Normalizing Flows with Stochastic Interpolants
keywords: normalizing flow; ODE; generative model
abstracts: A generative model based on a continuous-time normalizing flow between any pair of base and target probability densities is proposed. The velocity field of this flow is inferred from the probability current of a time-dependent density that interpolates between the base and the target in finite time. Unlike conventional normalizing flow inference methods based the maximum likelihood principle, which require costly backpropagation through ODE solvers, our interpolant approach leads to a simple quadratic loss for the velocity itself which is expressed in terms of expectations that are readily amenable to empirical estimation. The flow can be used to generate samples from either the base or target, and to estimate the likelihood at any time along the interpolant. In addition, the flow can be optimized to minimize the path length of the interpolant density, thereby paving the way for building optimal transport maps. In situations where the base is a Gaussian density, we also show that the velocity of our normalizing flow can also be used to construct a diffusion model to sample the target as well as estimate its score. However, our approach shows that we can bypass this diffusion completely and work at the level of the probability flow with greater simplicity, opening an avenue for methods based solely on ordinary differential equations as an alternative to those based on stochastic differential equations. Benchmarking on density estimation tasks illustrates that the learned flow can match and surpass conventional continuous flows at a fraction of the cost, and compares well with diffusions on image generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet $32 \times 32$. The method scales ab-initio ODE flows to previously unreachable image resolutions, demonstrated up to $128\times128$.
one_sentence_summary: A method is proposed to construct normalizing flows based on stochastic interpolants, yielding an efficient training algorithm compared to equivalent ODE methods, and providing a theoretical framework to map score based diffusions to ODEs.
standard_prompt: A novel generative model based on a continuous-time normalizing flow using stochastic interpolants offers advantages over traditional methods by avoiding complex optimization techniques like backpropagation and enabling direct sampling and likelihood estimation from both the base and target distributions, potentially reducing computational costs significantly compared to existing approaches.
cot_prompt: A novel generative model using a continuous-time normalizing flow achieves high-quality density estimation by inferring the velocity field directly from the interpolated probability current, demonstrating superior performance over traditional approaches while scaling efficiently to higher-resolution images.
dsp_prompt: A novel normalizing flow architecture using stochastic interpolation yields high-performance density modeling and sampling capabilities, outperforming traditional approaches while scaling efficiently to large image sizes.

titles: FSNet: Compression of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks by Filter Summary
keywords: Compression of Convolutional Neural Networks; Filter Summary CNNs; Weight Sharing
abstracts: We present a novel method of compression of deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by weight sharing through a new representation of convolutional filters. The proposed method reduces the number of parameters of each convolutional layer by learning a $1$D vector termed Filter Summary (FS). The convolutional filters are located in FS as overlapping $1$D segments, and nearby filters in FS share weights in their overlapping regions in a natural way. The resultant neural network based on such weight sharing scheme, termed Filter Summary CNNs or FSNet, has a FS in each convolution layer instead of a set of independent filters in the conventional convolution layer. FSNet has the same architecture as that of the baseline CNN to be compressed, and each convolution layer of FSNet has the same number of filters from FS as that of the basline CNN in the forward process. With compelling computational acceleration ratio, the parameter space of FSNet is much smaller than that of the baseline CNN. In addition, FSNet is quantization friendly. FSNet with weight quantization leads to even higher compression ratio without noticeable performance loss. We further propose Differentiable FSNet where the way filters share weights is learned in a differentiable and end-to-end manner. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FSNet in compression of CNNs for computer vision tasks including image classification and object detection, and the effectiveness of DFSNet is evidenced by the task of Neural Architecture Search.
one_sentence_summary: We present a novel method of compression of deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by weight sharing through a new representation of convolutional filters.
standard_prompt: Our novel approach, Filter Summary Network (FSNet), achieves significant compression of deep convolutional neural networks by leveraging filter summarization techniques, reducing parameter counts while maintaining performance comparable to traditional models through efficient weight sharing within convolutional layers.
cot_prompt: A novel filter summary technique for convolutional neural networks reduces parameter size and accelerates computation while maintaining high accuracy, offering both efficient parameter quantization and differentiation capabilities.
dsp_prompt: We introduce Filter Summary CNNs (FSNet), a novel approach for compressing deep convolutional neural networks using filter summaries, achieving significant computational efficiency while maintaining competitive accuracy through weight sharing within convolutional layers.

titles: Predicting Floor-Level for 911 Calls with Neural Networks and Smartphone Sensor Data
keywords: Recurrent Neural Networks; RNN; LSTM; Mobile Device; Sensors
abstracts: In cities with tall buildings, emergency responders need an accurate floor level location to find 911 callers quickly. We introduce a system to estimate a victim's floor level via their mobile device's sensor data in a two-step process. First, we train a neural network to determine when a smartphone enters or exits a building via GPS signal changes. Second, we use a barometer equipped smartphone to measure the change in barometric pressure from the entrance of the building to the victim's indoor location. Unlike impractical previous approaches, our system is the first that does not require the use of beacons, prior knowledge of the building infrastructure, or knowledge of user behavior. We demonstrate real-world feasibility through 63 experiments across five different tall buildings throughout New York City where our system predicted the correct floor level with 100% accuracy.
one_sentence_summary: We used an LSTM to detect when a smartphone walks into a building. Then we predict the device's floor level using data from sensors aboard the smartphone.
standard_prompt: A novel system uses smartphone sensors, including GPS and barometer, to accurately predict the floor-level location of victims entering tall buildings, achieving 100% accuracy in sixty-three experiments across five NYC skyscrapers.
cot_prompt: Our novel system predicts the floor level of victims calling 911 using smartphone sensors, achieving 100% accuracy by combining GPS changes and barometric pressure measurements.
dsp_prompt: A novel two-step system utilizing a recurrent neural network and smartphone sensors accurately predicts floor levels within buildings based on GPS and barometric pressure data, achieving perfect accuracy in real-world tests across multiple NYC skyscrapers.

titles: Mask and Understand: Evaluating the Importance of Parameters
keywords: influence function; interpretability; model pruning; feature importance ranking
abstracts: Influence functions are classic techniques from robust statistics based on first-order Taylor approximations that have been widely used in the machine learning community to estimate small perturbations of datasets accurately to the model. However, existing researches concentrate on the estimate the perturbations of the training or pre-training points. In this paper, we introduce the influence functions to predict the effects of removing features or parameters. It is worth emphasizing that our method can be applied to explore the influence of any combination of parameters disturbance on the model whether they belong to the same layer or whether are related. The validation and experiments also demonstrate that the influence functions for parameters can be used in many fields such as understanding model structure, model pruning, feature importance ranking, and any other strategies of masking parameters as you can imagine when you want to evaluate the importance of a group of parameters.
one_sentence_summary: We propose a parameter-based influence function which can be applied to explore the influence of any combination of parameters disturbance on the model whether they belong to the same layer or whether they are related.
standard_prompt: The study introduces influence functions to assess the impact of parameter removal on models, enabling their application across various domains including understanding model structure, parameter masking, and exploring parameter importance, highlighting its broad applicability in evaluating the significance of multiple parameters simultaneously.
cot_prompt: The study introduces influence functions to assess the impact of parameter removals across different layers within a neural network, highlighting its versatility for various applications including understanding model structure and feature importance ranking.
dsp_prompt: The study introduces influence functions to predict parameter effects and explores their applications in various ML tasks like model pruning and feature importance ranking, highlighting their versatility across different combinations of parameter disturbances.

titles: Combining Imitation and Reinforcement Learning with Free Energy Principle
keywords: Imitation; Reinforcement Learning; Free Energy Principle
abstracts: Imitation Learning (IL) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) from high dimensional sensory inputs are often introduced as separate problems, but a more realistic problem setting is how to merge the techniques so that the agent can reduce exploration costs by partially imitating experts at the same time it maximizes its return. Even when the experts are suboptimal (e.g. Experts learned halfway with other RL methods or human-crafted experts), it is expected that the agent outperforms the suboptimal experts’ performance. In this paper, we propose to address the issue by using and theoretically extending Free Energy Principle, a unified brain theory that explains perception, action and model learning in a Bayesian probabilistic way. We find that both IL and RL can be achieved based on the same free energy objective function. Our results show that our approach is promising in visual control tasks especially with sparse-reward environments.
one_sentence_summary: Extending Free Energy Principle to achieve imitation reinforcement learning for sparse reward problems with suboptimal experts
standard_prompt: Combining imitation learning and reinforcement learning through the Free Energy Principle yields superior performance for reducing exploration costs and achieving optimal outcomes in complex, suboptimal expert settings, particularly in sparse-reward environments.
cot_prompt: Our work combines Imitation Learning and Reinforcement Learning through the Free Energy Principle, demonstrating superior performance in complex tasks like visual control with sparse rewards.
dsp_prompt: The Free Energy Principle is applied to combine Imitation Learning and Reinforcement Learning for agents to optimize exploration while maximizing reward in complex environments, achieving superior outcomes compared to suboptimal expert guidance.

titles: Learning with AMIGo: Adversarially Motivated Intrinsic Goals
keywords: reinforcement learning; exploration; meta-learning
abstracts: A key challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) consists of learning in environments with sparse extrinsic rewards. In contrast to current RL methods, humans are able to learn new skills with little or no reward by using various forms of intrinsic motivation. We propose AMIGo, a novel agent incorporating -- as form of meta-learning -- a goal-generating teacher that proposes Adversarially Motivated Intrinsic Goals to train a goal-conditioned "student" policy in the absence of (or alongside) environment reward. Specifically, through a simple but effective "constructively adversarial" objective, the teacher learns to propose increasingly challenging -- yet achievable -- goals that allow the student to learn general skills for acting in a new environment, independent of the task to be solved. We show that our method generates a natural curriculum of self-proposed goals which ultimately allows the agent to solve challenging procedurally-generated tasks where other forms of intrinsic motivation and state-of-the-art RL methods fail.
one_sentence_summary: A "constructively adversarial" teacher-student setup can augment on-policy algorithms to better solve difficult exploration tasks in RL.
standard_prompt: AMIGo leverages adversarial goal generation to enable agents to learn complex skills autonomously, demonstrating its effectiveness in solving diverse procedural tasks.
cot_prompt: AMIGo introduces a goal-generation mechanism within a meta-learning framework, enabling agents to learn complex skills in the absence of traditional rewards through adversarial intrinsic goals, demonstrating superior performance over existing approaches in solving procedural tasks.
dsp_prompt: AMIGo leverages an adversarially motivated intrinsic goal generator to enable agents to autonomously learn complex skills in the absence of explicit rewards, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating a structured hierarchy of goals that enhances generalization across diverse and procedural environments.

titles: Distributionally Robust Optimization with Bias and Variance Reduction
keywords: stochastic optimization; convex optimization; distributionally robust learning; spectral risk measures; incremental optimization
abstracts: We consider the distributionally robust optimization (DRO) problem, wherein a learner optimizes the worst-case empirical risk achievable by reweighing the observed training examples. We present Prospect, a stochastic gradient-based algorithm that only requires tuning a single learning rate hyperparameter, and prove that it enjoys linear convergence for smooth regularized losses. This contrasts with previous algorithms that either require tuning multiple hyperparameters or potentially fail to converge due to biased gradient estimates or inadequate regularization. Empirically, we show that Prospect can converge 2-3x faster than baselines such as SGD and stochastic saddle-point methods on distribution shift and fairness benchmarks spanning tabular, vision, and language domains.
one_sentence_summary: We propose a linearly convergent stochastic (a.k.a. incremental) algorithm that optimizes spectral risk measures, which are distributionally robust objectives that include the superquantile.
standard_prompt: Prospect, a novel stochastic gradient algorithm, offers linear convergence for smooth DRO problems through optimal hyperparameter tuning, demonstrating superior performance over traditional methods on various datasets, including those addressing distribution shifts and fairness issues across different domains.
cot_prompt: Prospect, a single-learning-rate-stochastic-gradient algorithm, achieves superior convergence rates over existing DRO approaches through optimal hyperparameter tuning and reduced bias/variance in gradients.
dsp_prompt: Prospect, a novel stochastic gradient-based algorithm, efficiently converges linearly for smooth regularized losses through a simple single hyperparameter tuning, outperforming existing methods on distributional shifts and fairness across various domains, including tabular, visual, and textual data.

titles: Privacy Preserving Recalibration under Domain Shift
keywords: uncertainty calibration; differential privacy
abstracts: Classifiers deployed in high-stakes applications must output calibrated confidence scores, i.e. their predicted probabilities should reflect empirical frequencies. Typically this is achieved with recalibration algorithms that adjust probability estimates based on the real-world data; however, existing algorithms are not applicable in real-world situations where the test data follows a different distribution from the training data, and privacy preservation is paramount (e.g. protecting patient records). We introduce a framework that provides abstractions for performing recalibration under differential privacy constraints. This framework allows us to adapt existing recalibration algorithms to satisfy differential privacy while remaining effective for domain-shift situations. Guided by our framework, we also design a novel recalibration algorithm, accuracy temperature scaling, that is tailored to the requirements of differential privacy. In an extensive empirical study, we find that our algorithm improves calibration on domain-shift benchmarks under the constraints of differential privacy. On the 15 highest severity perturbations of the ImageNet-C dataset, our method achieves a median ECE of 0.029, over 2x better than the next best recalibration method and almost 5x better than without recalibration.
one_sentence_summary: We introduce a framework that provides abstractions for performing recalibration under differential privacy constraints, design a novel recalibration algorithm that works well in this setting, and extensively validate our method experimentally.
standard_prompt: We present a framework and new algorithm, accuracy temperature scaling, which adapts existing recalibration techniques under differential privacy conditions, improving calibration effectiveness across diverse datasets including ImageNet-C under varying levels of domain shift and privacy constraints.
cot_prompt: Our framework enables the adaptation of recalibration algorithms to maintain accurate confidence scoring during domain shifts while preserving privacy through differential privacy techniques, achieving superior performance compared to existing methods.
dsp_prompt: We propose a framework and new recalibration algorithm called accuracy temperature scaling that improve uncertainty calibration under differential privacy constraints, achieving significant improvements in domain-shift scenarios compared to existing methods.

titles: Learning Diverse Quadruped Locomotion Gaits via Reward Machines
keywords: Reward Machine; Quadruped Locomotion; Reinforcement Learning; Robotics
abstracts: Quadruped animals are capable of exhibiting a diverse range of locomotion gaits. While progress has been made in demonstrating such gaits on robots, current methods rely on motion priors, dynamics models, or other forms of extensive manual efforts. People can use natural language to describe dance moves. Could one use a formal language to specify quadruped gaits? To this end, we aim to enable easy gait specification and efficient policy learning. Leveraging Reward Machines~(RMs) for high-level gait specification over foot contacts, our approach is called RM-based Locomotion Learning~(RMLL), and supports adjusting gait frequency at execution time. Gait specification is enabled through the use of a few logical rules per gait (e.g., alternate between moving front feet and back feet) and does not require labor-intensive motion priors. Experimental results in simulation highlight the diversity of learned gaits (including two novel gaits), their energy consumption and stability across different terrains, and the superior sample-efficiency when compared to baselines. We also demonstrate these learned policies with a real quadruped robot.
one_sentence_summary: We specify and learn diverse quadruped locomotion gaits via Reward Machines, and deploy on hardware.
standard_prompt: Learning diverse quadruped locomotion gaits using reward machines enables easy specification and efficient policy learning, showcasing the versatility and efficiency of robotic locomotion.
cot_prompt: A new method using Reward Machines enables effective high-level gait specification and flexible policy learning for diverse quadruped locomotions, showcasing improved efficiency and versatility compared to traditional approaches.
dsp_prompt: RM-based Locomotion Learning (RMLL) enables efficient high-level gait specification using Reward Machines, showcasing diverse quadruped locomotion gaits in simulation and real-world applications.

titles: What Doesn't Kill You Makes You Robust(er): How to Adversarially Train against Data Poisoning
keywords: Data Poisoning; Poisoning Defenses; Adversarial Training; Empirical Defenses; Robustness; Security
abstracts:
Data poisoning is a threat model in which a malicious actor tampers with training data to manipulate outcomes at inference time. A variety of defenses against this threat model have been proposed, but each suffers from at least one of the following flaws: they are easily overcome by adaptive attacks, they severely reduce testing performance, or they cannot generalize to diverse data poisoning threat models.  Adversarial training, and its variants, are currently considered the only empirically strong defense against (inference-time) adversarial attacks.  In this work, we extend the adversarial training framework to defend against (training-time) data poisoning.  Our method desensitizes networks to the effects of such attacks by creating poisons during training and injecting them into training batches. 
We show that this defense withstands adaptive attacks, generalizes to diverse threat models, and incurs a better performance trade-off than previous defenses.
one_sentence_summary: Robust training is a good defense against targeted data poisoning, even for strong, adaptive attacks.
standard_prompt: Adversarial training, when adapted for defensive purposes, effectively mitigates data poisoning threats through desensitization, demonstrating superior performance over existing defenses while maintaining robustness against adaptive adversarial attacks across various scenarios.
cot_prompt: Adversarial training effectively mitigates data poisoning threats through desensitization techniques that enhance robustness and performance across various scenarios.
dsp_prompt: Adversarial training effectively mitigates the impact of data poisoning threats through the creation and incorporation of poisoned inputs during network training, enhancing robustness while maintaining favorable performance metrics compared to traditional defensive strategies.

titles: How does Contrastive Pre-training Connect Disparate Domains?
keywords: pre-training; contrastive learning; robustness; out-of-distribution; domain shift
abstracts: Pre-training on massive unlabeled datasets greatly improves accuracy under distribution shifts. As a first step toward understanding this, we study a popular pre-training method, contrastive learning, in the unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) setting where we only have labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled data from a target domain. We begin by showing on 4 benchmark datasets that out-of-the-box contrastive pre-training (even without large-scale unlabeled data) is competitive with other UDA methods. Intuitions from classical UDA methods such as domain adversarial training focus on bringing the domains together in feature space to improve generalization from source to target. Surprisingly, we find that contrastive pre-training learns features that are very far apart between the source and target domains. How then does contrastive learning improve robustness to distribution shift? We develop a conceptual model for contrastive learning under domain shifts, where data augmentations form connections between classes and domains that can be far apart. We propose a new measure of connectivity ---the relative connection strengths between same and different classes across domains---that governs the success of contrastive pre-training for domain adaptation in a simple example and strongly correlates with our results on benchmark datasets.
one_sentence_summary: Off-the-shelf contrastive pre-training is a competitive method for domain adaptation, and we develop a connectivity framework to understand how it learns representations that generalize across domains.
standard_prompt: Contrastive pre-training, despite its simplicity, exhibits strong performance on various UDA tasks through unique feature representation and enhanced class-domain connectivity driven by novel measures like relative connection strengths.
cot_prompt: Contrastive pre-training's unique feature of learning distinct representations between disparate domains leads to improved robustness against distributional shifts through enhanced class-domain connectivity measures.
dsp_prompt: Contrastive learning's ability to establish strong class-domain connections through data augmentation effectively improves transferability across disparate domains, despite its initial performance gap, demonstrating a novel approach to enhancing model robustness during out-of-distribution scenarios.

titles: Graph Deformer Network
keywords: Graph Convolution; Anchor Space; Anisotropic Convolution; Graph Classification; Node Classification
abstracts: Convolution learning on graphs draws increasing attention recently due to its potential applications to a large amount of irregular data. Most graph convolution methods leverage the plain summation/average aggregation to avoid the discrepancy of responses from isomorphic graphs. However, such an extreme collapsing way would result in a structural loss and signal entanglement of nodes, which further cause the degradation of the learning ability. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective graph deformer network (GDN) to fulfill anisotropic convolution filtering on graphs,  analogous to the standard convolution operation on images. Local neighborhood subgraphs (acting like receptive fields) with different structures are deformed into a unified virtual space, coordinated by several anchor nodes. In space deformation, we transfer components of nodes therein into anchors by learning their correlation, and build a pseudo multi-granularity plane calibrated with anchors. Anisotropic convolutional kernels can be further performed over the anchor-coordinated space to well encode local variations of receptive fields. By parameterizing anchors and stacking coarsening layers, we build a graph deformer network in an end-to-end fashion. Theoretical analysis indicates its connection to previous work and shows the promising property of isomorphism testing. Extensive experiments on widely-used datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed GDN in node and graph classifications.
one_sentence_summary: We propose an effective graph deformer network (GDN) to implement an anisotropic convolution filtering on graphs, and verify its superiority in theory and experiment.
standard_prompt: The authors introduce the Graph Deformer Network (GDN), a novel approach that simplifies convolutions on graphs by deforming local neighborhoods through a hierarchical process involving multiple anchor nodes and anisotropic kernel operations, demonstrating improved performance in classification tasks compared to traditional methods.
cot_prompt: The authors introduce the Graph Deformer Network (GDN), a novel framework for anisotropic convolution on graphs through deformable local neighborhoods, achieving better performance in classification tasks compared to traditional methods.
dsp_prompt: The authors introduce the Graph Deformer Network (GDN), a novel approach for performing anisotropic convolutions on graphs, leveraging anchor spaces to coordinate local neighborhoods and deform them into a unified virtual structure, thereby enhancing the representation capabilities of convolution operations on irregular data.

titles: Extreme Masking for Learning Instance and Distributed Visual Representations
keywords: visual representation learning; self-supervised learning; masked modeling
abstracts:
The paper presents a scalable approach for learning distributed representations over individual tokens and a holistic instance representation simultaneously. We use self-attention blocks to represent distributed tokens, followed by cross-attention blocks to aggregate the holistic instance. The core of the approach is the use of extremely large token masking (75\%-90\%) as the data augmentation for supervision. Our model, named ExtreMA, follows the plain BYOL approach where the instance representation from the unmasked subset is trained to predict that from the intact input. Learning requires the model to capture informative variations in an instance, instead of encouraging invariances. 
The paper makes three contributions: 1) Random masking is a strong and computationally efficient data augmentation for learning generalizable attention representations. 2) With multiple sampling per instance, extreme masking greatly speeds up learning and hungers for more data. 3) Distributed representations can be learned from the instance supervision alone, unlike per-token supervisions in masked modeling.
one_sentence_summary: A method that uses extremely large masking as a novel augmentation for learning siamese networks.
standard_prompt: Randomly masking a significant portion of tokens during training enhances generality and efficiency in learning distributed visual representations through self- and cross-attention mechanisms, achieving superior performance compared to traditional approaches like masked language models.
cot_prompt: The paper introduces ExtreMA, a novel method using random masking to learn distributed representations, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional approaches like masked modeling.
dsp_prompt: Extremely large token masking significantly enhances visual representation learning through self- and cross-attention mechanisms, enabling fast convergence with minimal labeled data and overcoming limitations in traditional supervised approaches.

titles: Minimalistic Unsupervised Representation Learning with the Sparse Manifold Transform
keywords: Unsupervised Learning; Sparsity; Low-rank; Manifold learning; Spectral Embedding
abstracts: We describe a minimalistic and interpretable method for unsupervised representation learning that does not require data augmentation, hyperparameter tuning, or other engineering designs, but nonetheless achieves performance close to the state-of-the-art (SOTA) SSL methods. Our approach leverages the sparse manifold transform, which unifies sparse coding, manifold learning, and slow feature analysis. With a one-layer deterministic (one training epoch) sparse manifold transform, it is possible to achieve $99.3\%$ KNN top-1 accuracy on MNIST, $81.1\%$ KNN top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10, and $53.2\%$ on CIFAR-100. With simple gray-scale augmentation, the model achieves $83.2\%$ KNN top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and $57\%$ on CIFAR-100. These results significantly close the gap between simplistic ``white-box'' methods and SOTA methods. We also provide visualization to illustrate how an unsupervised representation transform is formed. The proposed method is closely connected to latent-embedding self-supervised methods and can be treated as the simplest form of VICReg. Though a small performance gap remains between our simple constructive model and SOTA methods, the evidence points to this as a promising direction for achieving a principled and white-box approach to unsupervised representation learning, which has potential to significantly improve learning efficiency.
one_sentence_summary: We build a "white-box" unsupervised learning model with two parsimonious principles: sparsity and low-rankness, the model can be viewed as the simplest form of VICReg.
standard_prompt: Our minimalistic approach using the sparse manifold transform achieves high accuracy on various image datasets while maintaining simplicity, closing the gap between simpler models and state-of-the-art techniques in unsupervised representation learning.
cot_prompt: Our novel minimalistic method, leveraging the sparse manifold transform, achieves competitive performance across various datasets by combining simplicity with effective unsupervised representation learning techniques, demonstrating its potential for reducing complexity while maintaining high accuracy levels compared to state-of-the-art methods.
dsp_prompt: A novel minimalistic unsupervised representation learning method using the sparse manifold transform achieves high accuracy on various image datasets through a one-layer deterministic transform, closing the gap with state-of-the-art techniques by leveraging simplicity and interpretability.

titles: LLMatic: Neural Architecture Search via Large Language Models and Quality Diversity Optimization
keywords: Neural Architecture Search; Large Language Models; Quality Diversity Optimization
abstracts:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools capable of accomplishing a broad spectrum of tasks. Their abilities span numerous areas, and one area where they have made a significant impact is in the domain of code generation. Here, we propose to use the coding abilities of LLMs to introduce meaningful variations to code defining neural networks. Meanwhile, Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms are known to discover diverse and robust solutions. By merging the code-generating abilities of LLMs with the diversity and
robustness of QD solutions, we introduce LLMatic, a Neural Architecture Search (NAS) algorithm. While LLMs struggle to conduct NAS directly through prompts, LLMatic uses a procedural approach, leveraging QD for prompts and network architecture to create diverse and high-performing networks. We test LLMatic on the CIFAR-10 and NAS-bench-201 benchmark, demonstrating that it can produce competitive networks while evaluating just 2, 000 candidates, even without prior knowledge of the benchmark domain or exposure to any previous top-performing models for the benchmark.
one_sentence_summary: We introduce LLMatic that harnesses the power of Large Language Models and Quality Diversity Optimization to search neural architectures in efficient manner.
standard_prompt: Large Language Model capabilities enable innovative Neural Architecture Search methods like LLMatic, which combines the diversity discovery power of Quality-Diversity algorithms with the generative prowess of LLMs to efficiently search for diverse and high-performance neural network architectures across various benchmarks.
cot_prompt: Large Language Models (LLMs), combined with Quality-Diversity optimization, enable the creation of diverse and high-performance neural architectures through a novel method called LLMatic, showcasing its potential across domains including code generation and search.
dsp_prompt: Large Language Model capabilities are harnessed to develop a novel Neural Architecture Search method called LLMatic, which leverages Quality-Diversity optimization for diverse yet effective neural network architectures through large language model-generated prompts, showcasing its effectiveness across benchmark datasets including CIFAR-10 and NAS-bench-201.

titles: DSI++: Updating Transformer Memory with New Documents
keywords: Differentiable Search Index; Transformer Memory; Catastrophic Forgetting; Continual Learning; Lifelong Learning; Incremental Learning
abstracts:
Differentiable Search Indices (DSIs) encode a corpus of documents in the parameters of a model and use the same model to map queries directly to relevant document identifiers. Despite the solid performance of DSI models, successfully deploying them in scenarios where document corpora change with time is an open problem. In this work, we introduce DSI++, a continual learning challenge for DSI with the goal of continuously indexing new documents while being able to answer queries related to both previously and newly indexed documents. Across different model scales and document identifier representations, we show that continual indexing of new documents leads to considerable forgetting of previously indexed documents. We also hypothesize and verify that the model experiences forgetting events during training, leading to unstable learning. To mitigate these issues, we investigate two approaches. The first focuses on modifying the training dynamics. Flatter minima implicitly alleviates forgetting, so we explicitly optimize for flatter loss basins and show that the model stably memorizes more documents (+12\%).
Next, we introduce a parametric memory to generate pseudo-queries for documents and supplement them during incremental indexing to prevent forgetting for the retrieval task. Extensive experiments on a novel continual indexing benchmark based on Natural Questions demonstrate that our proposed solution mitigates the forgetting in DSI++ by a significant margin and improves the average Hits@10 by $+21.1\%$ over competitive baselines.
one_sentence_summary: We introduce DSI++, a continual learning challenge for DSI that requires incrementally adding documents to the model and propose a two-fold approach focusing on training dynamics and data-based regularization to enable it.
standard_prompt: DSI++ introduces two methods—flattening the loss landscape and generating pseudo-queries—to address continuous indexing challenges, showing improved stability and accuracy compared to traditional DSI models across various scale and representation variations.
cot_prompt: DSI++ introduces a continuous learning method to maintain and update transformer-based memory systems, showing improved query relevance and reduced forgetting through modifications to the training dynamics and the introduction of pseudo-queries.
dsp_prompt: Innovative solutions for DSI++ aim to address continuous document index updates and mitigate catastrophic forgetting through modified training dynamics and pseudo-query generation, achieving substantial improvements in query relevance across various datasets.

titles: Finite Depth and Width Corrections to the Neural Tangent Kernel
keywords: Neural Tangent Kernel; Finite Width Corrections; Random ReLU Net; Wide Networks; Deep Networks
abstracts: We prove the precise scaling, at finite depth and width, for the mean and variance of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) in a randomly initialized ReLU network. The standard deviation is exponential in the ratio of network depth to width. Thus, even in the limit of infinite overparameterization, the NTK is not deterministic if depth and width simultaneously tend to infinity. Moreover, we prove that for such deep and wide networks, the NTK has a non-trivial evolution during training by showing that the mean of its first SGD update is also exponential in the ratio of network depth to width. This is sharp contrast to the regime where depth is fixed and network width is very large. Our results suggest that, unlike relatively shallow and wide networks, deep and wide ReLU networks are capable of learning data-dependent features even in the so-called lazy training regime.
one_sentence_summary: The neural tangent kernel in a randomly initialized ReLU net is non-trivial fluctuations as long as the depth and width are comparable.
standard_prompt: We demonstrate that the neural tangent kernel's statistics scale exponentially with the ratio of network depth to width for deep and wide ReLU networks, highlighting their ability to learn data-dependent features despite being in the lazy training regime.
cot_prompt: We prove precise scaling properties of the neural tangent kernel for deep and wide ReLU networks, revealing non-determinism and evolving behavior during training.
dsp_prompt: The study reveals that the mean and variance of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) scale exponentially with the ratio of network depth to width, indicating that even in the limit of infinite overparameterization, the NTK's properties are not deterministic due to the presence of non-trivial dynamics during training.

titles: Learn, Unlearn and Relearn: An Online Learning Paradigm for Deep Neural Networks
keywords: warm-start; generalization; online learning; weight reinitialization; active forgetting; Anytime learning
abstracts: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are often trained with the premise that the complete training data set is provided ahead of time. However, in real-world scenarios, data often arrive in chunks over time. This leads to important considerations about the optimal strategy for training DNNs, such as whether to fine-tune them with each chunk of incoming data (warm-start) or to retrain them from scratch with the entire corpus of data whenever a new chunk is available. While employing the latter for training can be computationally inefficient, recent work has pointed out the lack of generalization in warm-start models. Therefore, to strike a balance between efficiency and generalization, we introduce Learn, Unlearn, and Relearn (LURE) an online learning paradigm for DNNs. LURE interchanges between the unlearning phase, which selectively forgets the undesirable information in the model through weight reinitialization in a data-dependent manner, and the relearning phase, which emphasizes learning on generalizable features. We show that our training paradigm provides consistent performance gains across datasets in both classification and few-shot settings. We further show that it leads to more robust and well-calibrated models.
one_sentence_summary: An efficient online learning paradigm which interchanges between the unlearning phase (selective forgetting) and relearning phase (retraining) to improve generalization of the DNNs through weight reinitialization.
standard_prompt: The Learn, Unlearn, and Relearn (LURE) framework enables efficient and effective training of deep neural networks by alternating between unlearning and relearning phases, achieving improved performance in various tasks compared to traditional methods.
cot_prompt: The Learn, Unlearn, and Relearn (LURE) framework demonstrates improved performance in deep neural network training by dynamically balancing learning and forgetting, enhancing both accuracy and robustness across various tasks.
dsp_prompt: The Learn, Unlearn, and Relearn (LURE) framework enables efficient online learning by dynamically balancing the trade-off between computational efficiency and model generalization through selective forgetting during the unlearning phase and enhanced learning during the relearning phase.

titles: BLOOM Large Language Models and the Chomsky Hierarchy
keywords: Large Language Models; Chomsky Hierarchy
abstracts: We study the performance of BLOOM large language models of different sizes on understanding 12 different languages from the Chomsky hierarchy using few-shot prompts. We investigate whether an increase in the complexity of the languages learned by the larger models can be characterized using the Chomsky hierarchy. We first show that prompting in BLOOM models enables reasoning with a good accuracy on language tasks as diverse as stack manipulation, string reversal, odds first, and interlocked pairing, when the queries are over short strings, that is, small bitwidth bit-vectors from the language. Second, we discover that the two largest models have the highest accuracy on such tasks for prompts with a fixed length, but smaller models are able to achieve similar accuracies with longer prompts. Unlike classical automata or grammar based approaches where algorithms for more complex languages in the Chomsky hierarchy can also recognize simpler languages, we find that the performance of the BLOOM large language models cannot be explained by the complexity of the languages in the Chomsky hierarchy.
one_sentence_summary: The performance of the BLOOM large language models cannot be explained by the complexity of the languages in the Chomsky hierarchy.
standard_prompt: BLOOM large language models excel at understanding diverse languages from the Chomsky hierarchy through few-shot prompts, demonstrating higher accuracy on tasks like stack manipulation and string operations compared to their counterparts, yet revealing limitations in capturing the full expressive power of the Chomsky hierarchy.
cot_prompt: BLOOM models demonstrate varying performances across different languages within the Chomsky hierarchy, highlighting challenges in explaining their capabilities through traditional computational models.
dsp_prompt: BLOOM large language models demonstrate varying performances across languages from the Chomsky hierarchy, highlighting limitations in explaining hierarchical complexities through algorithmic methods.

titles: Exploiting Certified Defences to Attack Randomised Smoothing
keywords: adversarial; attack; certified robustness; machine learning
abstracts: Certified guarantees of adversarial robustness play an important role in providing assurances regarding a models output, irrespective of the behaviour of an attacker. However, while the development of such guarantees has drawn upon an improved understanding of attacker behaviour, so too can certified guarantees be exploited in order to generate more efficient adversarial attacks. Within this work, we explore this heretofore undiscovered additional attack surface, while also considering how previously discovered attacks could be applied to models defended by randomised smoothing. In all bar one experiment our approach generates smaller adversarial perturbations for more than $70 \%$ of tested samples, reducing the average magnitude of the adversarial perturbation by $13 \%$.
one_sentence_summary: Certified defences can be used to attack the models they certify, yielding smaller adversarial perturbations
standard_prompt: Our study reveals that exploiting certified defenses against adversarial attacks enables generating significantly smaller perturbations, with over 70% of samples achieving reductions in adversarial perturbation size of up to 13%.
cot_prompt: Our study reveals that exploiting certified defenses against randomised smoothing can significantly reduce adversarial perturbations, achieving up to a 13% reduction in their magnitude for over 70% of test cases.
dsp_prompt: Our study reveals new ways to exploit certified defenses against adversarial attacks using randomised smoothing, achieving significant reductions in adversarial perturbation sizes for over 70% of test cases.

titles: Physical Gradients for Deep Learning
keywords: deep learning; simulation; optimization; inverse problems; physics
abstracts: Solving inverse problems, such as parameter estimation and optimal control, is a vital part of science. Many experiments repeatedly collect data and employ machine learning algorithms to quickly infer solutions to the associated inverse problems. We find that state-of-the-art training techniques are not well-suited to many problems that involve physical processes since the magnitude and direction of the gradients can vary strongly. We propose a novel hybrid training approach that combines higher-order optimization methods with machine learning techniques. We replace the gradient of the physical process by a new construct, referred to as the physical gradient. This also allows us to introduce domain knowledge into training by incorporating priors about the solution space into the gradients. We demonstrate the capabilities of our method on a variety of canonical physical systems, showing that physical gradients yield significant improvements on a wide range of optimization and learning problems.
one_sentence_summary: We present a new training technique for neural networks that interact with physical simulations, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques by orders of magnitude.
standard_prompt: A novel hybrid training approach using physical gradients significantly enhances performance across various inverse problems involving complex physical processes, improving both learning efficiency and accuracy through incorporation of prior knowledge and higher-order optimization.
cot_prompt: Our novel hybrid training approach using physical gradients significantly improves the performance of machine learning algorithms in solving inverse problems involving complex physical processes, demonstrating substantial benefits across various applications.
dsp_prompt: The authors propose a novel hybrid training approach combining high-order optimization with machine learning, leveraging physical gradients to improve training performance in inverse problems involving strong gradient variations.

titles: Uncertainty-aware Constraint Inference in Inverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning
keywords: Inverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning; Constrained Reinforcement Learning; Inverse Reinforcement Learning; Uncertainty Modeling
abstracts: Aiming for safe control, Inverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning (ICRL) considers inferring the constraints respected by expert agents from their demonstrations and learning imitation policies that adhere to these constraints. While previous ICRL works often neglected underlying uncertainties during training, we contend that modeling these uncertainties is crucial for facilitating robust constraint inference. This insight leads to the development of an Uncertainty-aware Inverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning (UAICRL) algorithm. Specifically, 1) aleatoric uncertainty arises from the inherent stochasticity of environment dynamics, leading to constraint-violating behaviors in imitation policies. To address this, UAICRL constructs risk-sensitive constraints by incorporating distributional Bellman updates into the cumulative costs model. 2) Epistemic uncertainty, resulting from the model's limited knowledge of Out-of-Distribution (OoD) samples, affects the accuracy of step-wise cost predictions. To tackle this issue, UAICRL develops an information-theoretic quantification of the epistemic uncertainty and mitigates its impact through flow-based generative data augmentation. Empirical results demonstrate that UAICRL consistently outperforms other baselines in continuous and discrete environments with stochastic dynamics. The code is available at https://github.com/Jasonxu1225/UAICRL.
one_sentence_summary: We proposed Uncertainty-aware Inverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning (UAICRL), a novel ICRL framework that models both the aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties towards uncertainty-aware constraint inference.
standard_prompt: Uncertainty-aware Inverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning (UAICRL), which integrates aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, enhances constraint inference and improves safety and performance in reinforcement learning tasks.
cot_prompt: Uncertainty-aware Constraint Inference in Inverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning enables more accurate constraint adherence and robustness against both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties in reinforcement learning, demonstrated through improved performance across various environments.
dsp_prompt: In UAI, an uncertainty-aware approach called UAICRL addresses two types of uncertainty - aleatoric and epistemic - by constructing risk-sensitive constraints and mitigating their effects using information-theoretic measures and flow-based augmentations, demonstrating superior performance in both continuous and discrete environments.

titles: Class-Context-Aware Phantom Uncertainty Modeling
keywords: uncertainty modeling; probabilistic representations; variation inference; robust learning
abstracts: Uncertainty modeling is crucial in developing robust and reliable models since it enables decision-makers to access the trustworthiness of predictions and make informed choices based on the uncertainty associated with the prediction. A straightforward approach to endow models with the ability to estimate uncertainty involves modeling a probabilistic distribution of the input representations and approximating it by variational inference. However, this method inevitably leads to an issue where uncertainty is underestimated, resulting in overconfident predictions even when dealing with data that contains inherent noise or ambiguity. In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called Class-Context-aware Phantom Uncertainty Modeling. To circumvent the problem of underestimating uncertainty associated with the input data, we shift the focus to infer the distribution of their respective phantoms, which are derived by leveraging class-contextual information. We mitigate the issue of uncertainty underestimation by demonstrating that the estimated uncertainty of the original input data is no less than that of the phantom. We showcase our method's superior robustness and generalization capabilities through experiments involving robust learning tasks such as noisy label learning and cross-domain generalization.
one_sentence_summary: We model the uncertainty of the artificial "phantoms" to mitigate uncertainty underestimation so as to improve model robustness.
standard_prompt: Class-Context-Aware Phantom Uncertainty Modeling addresses the challenge of underestimating uncertainty in models, introducing a novel approach that leverages class-contextual information to accurately quantify and generalize uncertainty across diverse domains.
cot_prompt: Class-Context-Aware Phantom Uncertainty Modeling addresses the challenge of overconfidence in uncertain predictions by shifting focus to infer the distribution of phantoms derived from class-contextual information, effectively mitigating uncertainty underestimation issues.
dsp_prompt: Class-Context-Aware Phantom Uncertainty Modeling addresses the challenge of underestimating uncertainty in probabilistic representation models by focusing on inferring the distribution of phantoms derived from class-contextual information, thereby enhancing the accuracy of uncertainty estimation and improving the robustness of predictive decisions.

titles: Adversarial Unlearning of Backdoors via Implicit Hypergradient
keywords: backdoor defense; backdoor removal; backdoor; minimax; implicit hypergradient
abstracts: We propose a minimax formulation for removing backdoors from a given poisoned model based on a small set of clean data. This formulation encompasses much of prior work on backdoor removal. We propose the Implicit Backdoor Adversarial Unlearning (I-BAU) algorithm to solve the minimax. Unlike previous work, which breaks down the minimax into separate inner and outer problems, our algorithm utilizes the implicit hypergradient to account for the interdependence between inner and outer optimization. We theoretically analyze its convergence and the generalizability of the robustness gained by solving minimax on clean data to unseen test data. In our evaluation, we compare I-BAU with six state-of-art backdoor defenses on eleven backdoor attacks over two datasets and various attack settings, including the common setting where the attacker targets one class as well as important but underexplored settings where multiple classes are targeted. I-BAU's performance is comparable to and most often significantly better than the best baseline. Particularly, its performance is more robust to the variation on triggers, attack settings, poison ratio, and clean data size. Moreover, I-BAU requires less computation to take effect; particularly, it is more than $13\times$ faster than the most efficient baseline in the single-target attack setting. Furthermore, it can remain effective in the extreme case where the defender can only access 100 clean samples---a setting where all the baselines fail to produce acceptable results.
one_sentence_summary: A minimax formulation of backdoor removal and an implicit gradient-based solver surpasses the state-of-art methods' best results in higher efficacy, efficiency, robustness to variations in triggers, settings, poison ratio, and clean data size.
standard_prompt: We present I-BAU, an algorithm that solves the minimax problem using implicit hypergradients, enabling adversarial unlearning of backdoors through a combination of clean data, resulting in improved robustness across different attack scenarios, including handling multiple target classes, varying attack settings, and limited clean data, demonstrating significant computational efficiency.
cot_prompt: The Implicit Backdoor Adversarial Unlearning (I-BAU) algorithm addresses the challenge of backdoor removal using a minimax formulation, leveraging implicit hypergradient to efficiently remove backdoors while maintaining high accuracy and computational efficiency across various attack scenarios.
dsp_prompt: We introduce I-BAU, an algorithm that uses implicit hypergradients to solve the minimax problem in adversarial unlearning, achieving superior performance compared to existing methods across different attack scenarios while requiring fewer computational resources.

titles: Distribution Based MIL Pooling Filters are Superior to Point Estimate Based Counterparts
keywords: multiple instance learning; mil; mil pooling filters; distribution pooling; point estimate based pooling
abstracts: Multiple instance learning (MIL) is a machine learning paradigm which learns the mapping between bags of instances and bag labels. There are different MIL tasks which can be solved by different MIL methods. One common component of all MIL methods is the MIL pooling filter, which obtains bag level representations from extracted features of instances. Here, we recommend and discuss a grouping scheme for MIL pooling filters: point estimate based pooling filters and distribution based pooling filters. The point estimate based pooling filters include the standard pooling filters, such as ‘max’, ‘mean’ and ‘attention’ pooling. The distribution based pooling filters include recently proposed ‘distribution’ pooling and newly designed ‘distribution with attention’ pooling. In this paper, we perform the first systematic analysis of different pooling filters. We theoretically showed that the distribution based pooling filters are superior to the point estimate based counterparts in terms of amount of information captured while obtaining bag level representations from extracted features. Then, we empirically study the performance of the 5 pooling filters, namely ‘max’, ‘mean’, ‘attention’, ‘distribution’ and ‘distribution with attention’, on distinct real world MIL tasks. We showed that the performance of different pooling filters are different for different MIL tasks. Moreover, consistent with our theoretical analysis, models with distribution based pooling filters almost always performed equal or better than that with point estimate based pooling filters.
one_sentence_summary: We performed the first systematic analysis of different MIL pooling filters and theoretically and experimentally showed that the distribution based pooling filters are superior to the point estimate based counterparts.
standard_prompt: Theoretical and empirical studies reveal that distribution-based multiple instance learning (MIL) pooling filters capture more information about bag-level representations compared to their point estimate counterparts across various MIL tasks.
cot_prompt: Theoretical and empirical studies reveal that distribution-based multiple-instance learning pooling filters significantly outperform their point-estimate counterparts, capturing more informative representations across various real-world multi-instance learning tasks.
dsp_prompt: Theoretical and empirical studies reveal that distribution-based MIL pooling filters outperform point estimate-based counterparts across various real-world multi-instance learning tasks, capturing more information during representation construction.

titles: Biased Multi-Domain Adversarial Training
keywords: adversarial training; adversarial robustness
abstracts: Several recent studies have shown that the use of extra in-distribution data can lead to a high level of adversarial robustness. However, there is no guarantee that it will always be possible to obtain sufficient extra data for a selected dataset. In this paper, we propose a biased multi-domain adversarial training (BiaMAT) method that induces training data amplification using freely available auxiliary datasets. The proposed method can achieve increased adversarial robustness on a primary dataset by leveraging auxiliary datasets via multi-domain learning. Specifically, data amplification on both robust and non-robust features can be accomplished through the application of BiaMAT as demonstrated through an additional analysis based on shuffle testing. Our experimental results indicate that BiaMAT can effectively utilize the robust and non-robust features present in various auxiliary datasets. Moreover, we demonstrate that while existing methods are vulnerable to negative transfer due to the distributional discrepancy between auxiliary and primary data, the proposed method enables neural networks to flexibly leverage diverse image datasets for adversarial training by successfully handling the domain discrepancy through the application of a confidence-based selection strategy.
one_sentence_summary: we propose a biased multi-domain adversarial training (BiaMAT) method that can achieve increased adversarial robustness on a primary dataset by leveraging auxiliary datasets via multi-domain learning.
